strengths: Novel and practically important problem: First systematic study of universal, transferable adversarial patches for VLAs in black-box settings with focus on cross-model and sim-to-real transfer

Theoretically grounded approach: Assumption 1 with linear alignment is empirically validated via CCA analysis; Proposition 1 and Corollary 1 provide principled justification for ℓ1 feature-space deviation

Well-designed VLA-specific components: Patch Attention Dominance targets action-relevant queries to avoid overfitting; Patch Semantic Misalignment uses cross-model probe phrases as anchors; Robustness-augmented bi-level optimization elegantly emulates adversarial training

Strong empirical results: 92+ percentage point drops in task success rates across diverse task categories (spatial, object, goal, long-horizon) in both simulated and physical settings, substantially outperforming RoboticAttack baselines
Comprehensive ablation studies: Table 3-4 demonstrate each component contributes meaningfully, with contrastive loss showing largest impact, validating theoretical emphasis on feature direction
Effective visualization of transferability: Figure 2 demonstrates UPA-RFAS learns universal patterns avoiding object mimicry, contrasting with baseline surrogate-overfitting
weaknesses: Incomplete submission with critical references to 'Appendix ??' for white-box results, π₀ transfer experiments, and proofs, severely hampering evaluation of core claims and reproducibility

Physical experiments lack clarity: Undefined whether 'Physical' results in Tables 1-2 are actual robot runs or simulation with domain randomization; no details on hardware setup, patch material, or illumination robustness—critical for robotics security claims
Limited victim model diversity undermines universality claims: Only tests OpenVLA variants and π₀; missing RT-1, ManipLLM, Octo, and other VLA architectures; π₀ results relegated to appendix

Theoretical assumptions validated only moderately: R² ≈ 0.654 means 35% of target variance unexplained; no empirical measurement of residual bound εE, smallest singular value σmin(A*), or sensitivity analysis across surrogate-victim pairs

Predetermined patch placement constrains generality: Sites predetermined for each suite to avoid object occlusion; reduces continuous placement space to discrete set with no ablation on placement restriction impact

VLA-specific loss components lack principled justification: PAD loss (Eq. 16) has three hyperparameters (λ, m) with one-sided ReLU penalty appearing ad-hoc; PSM loss (Eq. 18) uses LogSumExp without justifying over symmetric contrastive alternatives; design appears empirically driven rather than theoretically motivated

Missing hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: Only probe phrasing studied (Table 4); no ablations for perturbation budget εσ, bi-level balance (I vs K), temperatures τ, margin m, or weights λPAD, λPSM, making robustness and reproducibility unclear

Bi-level optimization details incomplete: Convergence guarantees, computational cost (I×K inner-outer loop complexity per batch), and whether inner loop truly emulates distributional shift vs. local worst-case not discussed

Geometric transformation distribution T undefined: Section 3.1 states Tt ~ T but formal specification missing; unclear how position, skew, rotation are sampled and sensitivity to T distribution unknown despite claims of robustness

Limited experimental scope: Only manipulation tasks studied; generalization to navigation or perception-only VLAs unknown; patch size sensitivity not systematically studied; only RoboticAttack baseline compared (no other transfer attack methods)

Defense discussion absent: Minimal beyond 'baseline for future defenses'; lacks concrete suggestions for mitigation (input preprocessing, certified robustness, attention monitoring), limiting impact vision

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: universal, transferable adversarial patches for VLA robots in black-box settings with practical safety implications.
Comprehensive multi-component framework thoughtfully integrating feature-space objectives, attention hijacking, and semantic steering with principled design.
Extensive experiments spanning multiple VLA variants (OpenVLA-7B, OpenVLA-oft, π0), real-world datasets (BridgeData V2, LIBERO), and both simulated and physical deployments.
Provides theoretical grounding with Assumption 1 on linear alignment and Proposition 1 establishing lower bounds on target-side deviations.
Ablation studies (Tables 3-4) systematically validate component contributions and probe sensitivity analysis.
Achieves significant degradation in simulated settings (5.75% success from 98.25% benign in Table 1), demonstrating attack potency in controlled conditions.
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Manuscript appears incomplete with multiple broken appendix references ('Appendix ??') throughout, including the crucial Proposition 1 proof. This prevents proper technical verification.
Weak theoretical justification: Assumption 1 relies on linear alignment but R² ≈ 0.654 means 34.6% of variance is unexplained. Implications of residual coupling (εE) not discussed.

Mixed and inconsistent transfer results contradict universality claims: In Table 2 physical setting, proposed method achieves 61.50% success degradation vs. TMA7 baseline at 90.25%. Simulated 'long' task shows 3% success identical to baselines with no explanation for failure.

Severe probe dependency (Table 4): Changing from {Action+Direction} to {Direction only} probes increases success from 61.50% to 75% (13.5 point swing), indicating brittleness and undermining generalizability claims.

Marginal improvements from complex components: RUPA bi-level optimization adds computational overhead for only 0.75 point improvement (62.25% vs. 61.50%); PAD loss provides only 1 point gain; primarily Jtr drives performance.

'Universal' transfer claim is oversold: Method works primarily within OpenVLA variants; transfer to fundamentally different π0 architecture substantially degrades (relegated to missing appendix). Limited to 2-3 VLA families.

Unfair baseline comparisons: RoboticAttack [49] methods weren't designed for cross-architecture transfer. No comparisons with transfer-focused attacks or defenses. Missing white-box performance comparisons.
Reproducibility gaps: Hyperparameters (λcon, λPAD, λPSM, ηδ, ησ, I, K) not fully specified. No code availability mentioned. Implementation details for attention extraction pipeline sparse.

Incomplete evaluation: No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals. Success Rate is binary and masks failure modes (wrong object, location, collisions). Physical experiment scope unclear (trial counts not reported).

Design choices not justified: How were hyperparameters selected? Why is clean-run attention a reliable proxy for action relevance across models? How were predetermined patch placement sites chosen? What is computational cost vs. baselines?
Physical realizability concerns: Smooth gradient patches difficult to print/apply physically. No discussion of patch durability, robustness to wear, lighting variations, or material choices.
Limited architecture diversity: Tests primarily OpenVLA family and π0. No evaluation on Octo, RT-2, GATO, or other VLA architectures mentioned in related work.
No defense discussion: Claims to provide 'baseline for future defenses' but offers zero defense mechanisms or analysis of potential mitigations.
Presentation issues: Dense Figure 1, notation inconsistencies (δ vs. δs), missing implementation details for CCA and linear regression pipelines. Reads as draft-stage submission.

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First systematic study of universal, transferable adversarial patches for VLA-driven robots under practical black-box conditions, addressing an important safety concern for deployed robotic systems.

Technically comprehensive methodology: Well-motivated combination of feature-space objectives, robustness-augmented bi-level optimization, and VLA-specific components. Proposition 1 provides theoretical grounding for ℓ1 deviation transferability.

Strong empirical results: Achieves dramatic success rate reductions (92+ points in simulation, 40.25% vs 98.25% benign) across multiple VLA models (OpenVLA, OpenVLA-oft variants), task suites, and sim-to-real transfer—substantially outperforming baseline objectives.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple surrogate-target pairs, evaluation on both LIBERO simulation and BridgeData V2 physical settings, extensive ablation studies (Tables 3-4), and informative patch visualizations showing avoidance of overfitting patterns.
Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with effective figures (Figures 1-2) that clearly communicate the framework architecture, training procedure, and design differences from baselines.
Practical focus: Addresses real-world threat model with predetermined patch placement and geometric randomization, demonstrating feasibility of physical attacks.
weaknesses: Weak theoretical foundation: Assumption 1 (linear alignment with bounded residual) is strong but only partially validated—reported R² ≈ 0.654 indicates 36.6% residual variance unexplained by linear map. No formal analysis of when this assumption fails or how violations affect transferability guarantees.

Limited transfer scope within diverse architectures: Primary evaluation uses OpenVLA-7B to OpenVLA-oft variants sharing common backbones. Transfer to π₀ (fundamentally different architecture) is mentioned as in appendix but not shown in main paper, weakening claims of universality across heterogeneous VLA designs.

Incomplete ablation on critical design choices: (i) Multiple hyperparameters (λcon, λPAD, λPSM, τ, m) lack sensitivity analysis; (ii) Choice of L1 over L2 deviation insufficiently justified—ablation shows modest impact; (iii) Contrastive loss dominance (Table 3: w/o Lcon shows 70.75% vs 61.50%) lacks deep explanation of why CCA-aligned directions transfer better.

Task-specific probe selection requiring manual design: Text probes need action verbs and spatial directions chosen per-task. While Table 4 shows impact, the paper lacks systematic guidance for selecting probes for novel tasks or formal analysis of generalizability to unseen task types.

Significant sim-to-real performance gap inadequately addressed: Physical success rates substantially lower than simulated (61.50% vs 43.50% for OpenVLA-oft transfer). Limited discussion of domain shift causes or mitigation strategies; only one physical dataset evaluated.

Incomplete submission and reproducibility concerns: Multiple appendix references marked '??' prevent verification of claimed results (white-box performance, π₀ transfer, proof of Proposition 1). Missing details on computational cost, training time, hyperparameter selection rationale, and no mention of code availability.

Limited analysis of attack mechanisms: (i) Patch visualizations (Figure 2) lack interpretation of exploited features; (ii) No attention maps or saliency visualizations showing what representations PAD/PSM hijack; (iii) No failure case analysis or discussion of which task types are most vulnerable.

Modest component-level novelty: L1 deviation, InfoNCE, and attention-based objectives are established techniques. Novelty primarily lies in domain-specific combination rather than methodological innovation. Connection between theoretical framework (Assumption 1, Proposition 1) and VLA-specific losses (PAD, PSM) is not rigorously established.

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests on reported success rates. Unclear whether performance differences are statistically significant or within noise margins.

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Only compares against RoboticAttack [49], the sole prior VLA patch attack work. Missing comparisons to adapted general adversarial transferability techniques (gradient masking, ensemble methods) or other black-box attack strategies.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine security gap in VLA robustness; existing work focuses on white-box attacks while this work systematically studies universal, transferable patch attacks in realistic black-box settings with architectural variance and sim-to-real shifts

Strong theoretical foundation: Assumption 1 (linear feature alignment) is empirically validated using CCA and linear regression; Propositions 1 and Corollary 1 rigorously justify why ℓ1 deviation ensures target-side transfer

Comprehensive technical framework seamlessly integrating feature-space objectives (ℓ1 + repulsive InfoNCE), robustness-augmented bi-level optimization, and two novel VLA-specific losses (PAD, PSM) with clear motivation for each component

Strong and consistent empirical results across diverse settings: dramatic success rate reduction (98.25% → 5.75% in simulation, 98.25% → 40.25% in physical on OpenVLA-oft-w), consistent outperformance over baselines across all model variants and task types

Comprehensive experimental validation with proper ablations (Tables 2-3, Appendix E) demonstrating necessity of each component; multiple surrogate-victim pairs; evaluation on both simulation and real robot platforms
Good reproducibility: detailed algorithm (Alg. 1), extensive implementation details (Appendix B), hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Appendix E), and promise of code release
weaknesses: Significant simulation-to-real performance degradation: 98.25% → 40.25% physical success (8.5× weaker than simulated 5.75%), undermining practical threat claims; real-world evaluation remains qualitative with only 3 tasks × 3 trials and no quantitative success metrics

Limited scope of black-box transfer: primary experiments focus on OpenVLA-family models; π₀ evaluation remains within VLA ecosystem; no evaluation against fundamentally different architectures (e.g., diffusion-based or RL-enhanced VLAs); predetermined patch placement overstates universality

Theoretical gaps in feature-space assumptions: R² ≈ 0.654 for linear alignment shows moderate empirical support with substantial residual variance not characterized; connection between feature-space transfer success and policy-level failure assumed rather than formally established

High method complexity with limited computational analysis: four weighted loss components plus robustness parameters; bi-level optimization adds computational overhead (8 inner + 50 outer steps) not compared to baselines; hyperparameter sensitivity not exhaustively studied across combinations

Binary evaluation metric (success rate) lacks nuance; no analysis of failure magnitude or task-dependent vulnerability; patch encoding and semantics not deeply analyzed; limited to manipulation tasks with unknown generalization to navigation or assembly

Limited threat model discussion: no analysis of patch detectability, potential defenses, or failure cases; responsible disclosure not addressed; probe phrase selection for PSM (Table 3) tested on only two alternatives despite importance shown in ablations
